vignette:
He is a 55-year-old man of Oceania descent who has spent much of his adult life caring for other people’s children, a role that suits him because he is patient, observant, and comfortable with routines. When he first talks about his life now, he returns again and again to the same point: everything changed the afternoon his adult daughter was injured in a violent assault. He had never imagined that something like that could happen to his family, and in the weeks after, the world feels to him as if it has become permanently less safe and less predictable.

Before the event, he is already living alone after a difficult divorce. The separation has left him guarded, but he keeps working because children give him a sense of purpose and structure. He likes the simple rhythms of his job as a nanny: school pickups, snack time, reading stories, calming tears, remembering whose jacket belongs to whom. He has always prided himself on being steady. People around him describe him as dependable, the kind of man who notices when a child is quiet for too long or when something is off in a household.

The assault on his daughter arrives without warning. He describes the moment he learns of it as if the air leaves the room. He is not with her when it happens, which he experiences as its own kind of injury. At the hospital, he sees bruises, tubes, and the stillness in her face before she fully wakes. He remembers holding her hand and feeling how small it suddenly seems, though she is an adult. From that point forward, he says, he starts living in two places at once: in the hospital room and in every moment that follows.

In the first days after the trauma, he moves through practical tasks almost automatically. He answers calls, speaks to police, informs relatives, and tries to keep his voice calm. But inside, he feels split open. He cannot sleep for more than a few hours at a time, and when he does drift off, he jolts awake in panic. He begins to replay the sequence of events obsessively, imagining what might have happened if he had answered the phone sooner, if he had insisted she come home earlier, if he had somehow been there. These thoughts circle endlessly, each one ending in the same place: he should have prevented it.

Over time, the fear spreads beyond the immediate event. He becomes hyperalert in public, scanning faces, exits, and parked cars. As a nanny, he notices himself standing closer to the children in his care than before, counting them repeatedly on outings, tightening his grip on small hands when crowds gather. He tells himself he is being responsible, but he also knows he is frightened. Sudden noises make him flinch. A raised voice can send a wave of heat through his body and leave his heart pounding. He avoids news reports, police dramas, and even certain streets that remind him of the hospital route he took in those first days. He no longer answers some calls right away because he fears bad news.

He also feels changed in his relationships. His divorce had already made him wary of depending on others, and the assault deepens that distrust. He finds it hard to talk about his daughter’s injuries without feeling overwhelmed, so he keeps conversations brief. Friends who mean well tell him she is alive, that she is safe now, that time will help. He hears their words but feels disconnected from them, as if they are speaking from a great distance. There are moments when he sits alone after work and feels nothing at all, followed by sudden surges of grief that arrive so quickly he has to leave the room. He misses being the kind of man who could comfort others without trembling inside.

Even now, months later, he remains tethered to the event. His daughter is recovering, but he cannot yet feel relief in a lasting way. He still checks locks multiple times at night. He keeps his phone beside him in bed and wakes at the smallest sound. At work, he functions well on the surface, but he describes himself as constantly bracing, as though another blow could come at any moment. He wants to be present for the children he cares for and for his daughter, yet much of his energy goes into managing fear, guilt, and the sense that the world has become dangerous in a way he cannot fully undo.
